query: Automotive suppliers tariff engineering customs classification

statements.text: Carrington Co. v. United States, the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals (“CCPA”) said “it is a well-established principle that classification of an imported article must rest upon its condition as imported.”

Merritt v. Welsh, held that tariff engineering is an acceptable practice.

Between 2009 and 2013, Ford imported over 160,000 Transit Connect vehicles. Before importation, Ford installed second-row seats in order to classify them as passenger cars, which carried a 2.5% tariff rate, avoiding the high tariff rate of 25% for transport vehicles.

Therefore, US customs authorities later reclassified these vehicles as transport vehicles based on their features and intended use. This reclassification led to allegations of false declarations by Ford, potentially resulting in over $1 billion in additional tariffs.
As part of the settlement, Ford agreed to pay $365 million to resolve the DOJ action.

Last year, Ford settled the dispute by agreeing to pay $365 million and committed to obtaining binding customs rulings for future models, while also withdrawing its lawsuit challenging the classification.
As background, Ford manufactured the Transit Connect vehicles in Turkey and imported them into the United States.
